Target networks

In Q-learning with a network, the target $r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')$ moves every time the weights move, so each update chases a target it has just pushed away. DQN computes targets with a frozen copy of the weights and refreshes the copy only every $C$ updates.

Baird's counterexample from Lesson 65, with all three legs of the triad switched on: the same features, $\gamma = 0.99$, $\alpha = 0.01$ and off-policy semi-gradient TD(0). The only change is that targets use frozen weights $\mathbf{w}^-$, copied from $\mathbf{w}$ every $C$ steps. $C = 1$ is the plain method of Lesson 65.

The maths

DQN's target uses the frozen weights $\boldsymbol\theta^-$ (Mnih et al., 2015):

$$y = r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \boldsymbol\theta^-), \qquad \boldsymbol\theta^- \leftarrow \boldsymbol\theta \text{ every } C \text{ updates}.$$

Between copies, $y$ does not depend on $\boldsymbol\theta$. Each phase is then ordinary regression onto fixed targets, true gradient descent on a fixed loss, with no feedback from the weights to the targets.

If every phase ran to convergence, phase $k+1$ would find the best fit to the targets made from phase $k$:

$$\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_s d(s)\,\Big[\,\mathbb{E}_\pi\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma \hat v(S_{t+1}, \mathbf{w}_k) \mid S_t = s\big] - \hat v(s, \mathbf{w})\Big]^2 .$$

That is value iteration with a regression step in the middle, often called fitted value iteration. It converges whenever "apply the Bellman backup, then fit" shrinks distances.

In Baird's example it does. Under $\pi$ every next state is the bottom one with reward 0, so every target is $\gamma \hat v(7, \mathbf{w}^-)$. With 8 weights and 7 states the features can fit any 7 values exactly, so after a long phase every state's value is about $\gamma \hat v(7, \mathbf{w}^-)$. Each copy therefore multiplies the values by about $\gamma = 0.99$, which is why large $C$ settles slowly but surely. (The first phase lifts the top states from 3 to about $0.99 \times 12$, so the RMS rises above its start before it shrinks.) With small $C$ the regression never finishes before the target moves, and the weights still run away.

It is not a cure. In Lesson 65's two-state example, fitting the first state's value $w$ to the target $2\gamma w^-$ gives

$$w_{k+1} = 2\gamma\, w_k,$$

which still diverges for $\gamma > 0.5$. The target network only makes it grow once per copy instead of a little every step. In the ablation of Mnih et al. (2015), removing the target network lowered the score on all five games tested. Removing replay instead hurt more on four of the five.

A smooth alternative, from DDPG (Lillicrap et al., 2016), is to move the copy a little every step: $\boldsymbol\theta^- \leftarrow \tau \boldsymbol\theta + (1 - \tau)\boldsymbol\theta^-$ with small $\tau$.
